altHeadlines: Brave Golfer Admits Crushing Toll Of Winning Basically Everything
Trophy Engraver Offered Counselling After Eighth Straight 'McIlroy'

body:
**DUBAI** — A local man broke down in tears on Sunday after being formally recognised as the best at golf for the eighth time, telling gathered reporters he was "emotional and proud" of his years-long struggle with sustained professional excellence.

Rory McIlroy, 36, clinched the Race to Dubai — the European tour's season-long prize for being the most consistent person in the field — drawing level with the all-time record of eight titles set by Scotland's Colin Montgomerie, the previous record holder for Most Career Tears Shed Adjacent To Silverware.

The Northern Irishman was visibly moved while reflecting on the burden of being extremely good at his job for nearly two decades, pausing several times to compose himself in what tour officials described as "the longest he has stood still all year."

"It takes a real toll," said a tour spokesperson, who asked not to be named because he was also welling up. "Most people will never understand what it's like to wake up every morning, fly to a beautiful golf course, and be measurably better at it than everyone else. It's a loneliness money cannot fix, though it has made several credible attempts."

Fellow competitors have rallied around McIlroy in what one analyst described as "a difficult period for a man who keeps winning." A peer support group, Excellence Anonymous, has reportedly been established on tour for players suffering from chronic success, though meetings remain poorly attended as most members keep winning things and have to leave early for ceremonies.

Tournament organisers confirmed the official trophy engraver, now in his eighth consecutive year of spelling 'McIlroy' correctly, has been offered grief counselling and a commemorative apron.

Back home in Holywood, County Down — a town that has won roughly five fewer major championships than its most famous resident — locals observed a minute's applause before returning to their pints. "We see him cry at this stage most years," said one man in a pub who declined to give his name but confirmed he was "class at crazy golf in the nineties." "Fair play to him. It can't be easy, being handed large trophies and enormous cheques all the time. I cried myself last Tuesday and nobody gave me a dime."

The tour has announced next year's trophy will feature a small absorbent shoulder for McIlroy to cry on, plus an extended plinth to accommodate the money.

At press time, McIlroy had been moved to a quiet area where officials confirmed he was resting comfortably among his eight season-long titles, five major championships and a bonus cheque sources described as "enormous, but no substitute for peace."
